analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims and their families sue the makers and sellers of untraceable ghost guns.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor and never received a vote in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given people injured by ghost guns — and families of people killed by them — the right to sue in federal court for damages against whoever made any component of the weapon or helped sell it. A ghost gun is a firearm without a serial number, typically assembled from kits or parts so it cannot be traced. States and local governments could also sue. It was introduced by one House Democrat, never picked up a cosponsor, and was referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured by ghost guns and the families of those killed by them would gain a new way to recover damages in court, and states and local governments could sue over the costs those shootings impose. Communities hit by untraceable crime guns would benefit from a financial deterrent on the kit makers and online sellers who currently face little consequence when their parts end up in weapons used in crimes.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a federal private right of action: an individual injured by a ghost gun, or a family member of someone killed by one, can sue the maker of any component of the gun or anyone who facilitated its sale for damages, including consequential damages [S3].
The right to sue also extends to states and their political subdivisions, allowing governments to recover costs from ghost gun makers and sellers [S3].

A ghost gun is defined as a firearm lacking a serial number engraved or cast by a licensed manufacturer or importer, and the bill covers parts designed to be assembled into such firearms — the kit-and-parts trade that today operates with little legal exposure [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ghost gun kit and parts makers, and retailers or other people who facilitate ghost gun sales, would bear new court-ordered damages and the cost of defending lawsuits. Defensive litigation risk could push some makers and sellers out of the market or toward serial-numbered, traceable products.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ghost gun kit makers and sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill reaches 'any person who facilitated any sale' of a ghost gun, language broad enough to sweep in people with only a peripheral role in a transaction, not just manufacturers and dealers [S3].

Litigation is a slow and indirect tool: lawsuits after a shooting do not prevent the next one, and a court-determined damages award is less predictable than a regulatory rule requiring serialization at the point of manufacture [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the affirmative defenses are narrow — covering only lawful self-defense and law enforcement — so the bill imposes strict, no-fault-style liability on the parts trade, which critics would call unfair to lawful sellers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but conditional: victims and families who today have little recourse against untraceable gun makers would get a path to court. The cost falls on the ghost gun parts industry, which is the point — the bill's design uses lawsuits as the deterrent, since Congress did not simply ban the kits. The main design weaknesses are the broad 'facilitated any sale' language and the fact that damages arrive only after someone has been hurt or killed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, never got a hearing or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) introduced the bill on June 9, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the complete action history shows only introduction and the committee referral [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over the life of the Congress [S4].
The House Judiciary Committee never scheduled action on the bill, so it never reached the House floor for a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Makers and sellers of ghost gun kits and parts are better off, because they face no new liability from lawsuits brought by shooting victims or their families. Shooting victims and grieving families gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ghost gun kit makers and sellers

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a private right of action against ghost gun component makers and sale facilitators; it attracted no other sponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 9, 2023 and took no action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: 0 of 216 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Not a single House member, including fellow Democrats, cosponsored the bill during its 18 months in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough support to reveal a partisan split: it had one sponsor and zero cosponsors, and the committee dominated by the opposing party never acted on it.

industries.industry: Ghost gun kit and parts makers
industries.note: The bill would let shooting victims and families sue any maker of a ghost gun component for damages, exposing the kit-and-parts trade to potentially ruinous liability. These businesses profit from selling unserialized firearm parts that cannot be traced when recovered at crime scenes.

Anyone who 'facilitated any sale' of a ghost gun could be sued, adding litigation risk for retailers and peer-to-peer sellers. Traceable, serial-numbered firearms would be unaffected, so the bill pushes sales toward the regulated, serialized market.
